newsitem.title: YUGOSLAVIA: Serbia privatisation to go on despite legal delay.
newsitem.headline: Serbia privatisation to go on despite legal delay.

text.p: Serbian government is determined to launch its privatisation programme, involving 5,000 firms valued at almost $56 billion, even though it is still waiting for parliament to approve a new privatisation law, a senior official said on Friday.

"Delay in adopting the (privatisation) law prevents us from working on a number of by-laws. But this will not cause any delays in launching the privatisation process on October 31," Serbian deputy privatisation minister Miroljub Hadzic told Reuters.

The new privatisation law was sent to parliament early in July but has so far failed to make it to the agenda as deputies continue to debate a series of election laws to which the opposition Democratic Party alone submitted more than 1,800 amendments.
Hadzic did not expect any amendments to the privatisation law even though it has been criticised by economists, businesses and opposition political parties.
The government prevented the opposition from submitting any amendments to the law when it abruptly scheduled the third reading without leaving the usual three-day period before the session.

The securities law will be changed because shareholders will not be given shares but a personal number serving as a code in a central depository stock account, a computerised system containing data on firms and shareholders, Hadzic said.
But the computerised register was seen opening fresh staff problems to the tiny ministry currently employing 10 people.
"At the moment there are no such experts in Yugoslavia. We have also sought external financial help, but we primarily need someone to show us how it works," Hadzic said.
The ministry had asked a French bourse to deliver its specialised software performing successfully in the Polish and the Hungarian central depository stock accounts.

The ministry also worked out a future marketing strategy for the privatisation process and is currently negotiating with a local marketing company on future posters, slogans and brochures to inform on privatisation progress and educate companies and workers on their rights in the process.

Hadzic also said a list of companies to be privatised under a special government programme may be halved to around 25 firms which qualify for a special state care by strategic importance, number of employees and size of debts.
